extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media scholars, students, and general readers interested in journalism and media ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and describe the criteria and usages that distinguish 'creative journalism' from other journalistic practices, including ethical boundaries, stylistic overlaps with creative writing, and forms of presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: creative enhancement with possible intent
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative journalism refers to a journalistic story than has been enhanced in a creative way by the journalist, possibly with an intent to mislead or with an objective to cause an event to happen that otherwise would not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This frames creative journalism both as stylistic enhancement and as potentially having problematic intents (misleading readers or instigating events). Use of the term can thus carry ethical implications about intent and outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlap with creative writing (feature/narrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: One usage of the term creative journalism is to cover an overlap between creative writing and journalism that occurs in the feature writing, narrative literature and whatever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalism is described here as the factual portrayal of news and events with minimal analysis and interpretation; by contrast 'creative' is original, expressive and imaginative. This criterion highlights when journalistic work adopts literary techniques (narrative, imaginative expression) and thus how to judge boundary between factual reporting and literary storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cudlipp's 'making news' standard (causing events vs fabricating)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hugh Cudlipp has defined creative journalism differently, as 'the art of causing something to occur that would not otherwise materialise' and the antithesis of the 'phantom scoop' where the foretold event does not occur. He also puts it as 'making news not faking news.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this criterion creative journalism is evaluated by whether the journalist's actions legitimately bring about real events (making news) rather than inventing or fabricating events (phantom scoop). It emphasizes outcomes and truthfulness of the eventual occurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative presentation (visual/photo/graphic journalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative journalism can be applied to a journalistic work that has creative presentation. Used this way it will often be used to denote a praiseworthy example of photojournalism, visual journalism or graphic journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion judges creative journalism positively when creativity is in presentation—visual design, photography, graphics—adding value or excellence without necessarily altering factual substance. It signals an editorial/esthetic standard rather than ethical concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euphemistic use implying deliberate misleading (creative as in 'creative accounting')
rubrics_metrics.description: The euphemism for 'creative journalism' refers to the similar use of 'creative' in 'creative accounting'. Here creative is used in the sense to mislead. The term has elements of relationship to tabloid journalism, yellow journalism and fakes news, though there are differences in emphasis and objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion treats 'creative' as a euphemism that may obscure dishonest practices. Evaluation under this standard considers whether 'creative' functions as a cover for deceptive reporting, and contrasts it with related phenomena (tabloid, yellow journalism, fake news) while noting differing emphases. (The article notes a significant difference from clickbait in emphasis/form.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative/absence criterion: not simply source error or unintentional spin
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative journalism does not occur when the source(s) are incorrect or as a result of spin propaganda providing the journalist has not knowingly colluded or negligently failed to check sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This defines a boundary: mistakes arising from bad sources or unintentional spin are not 'creative journalism' so long as the journalist did not knowingly collude or negligently fail to verify. Evaluation should consider journalist intent and reasonable diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology as provisional label for emergent genres
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative journalism has sometimes been applied to newly identified genres until a definitive designation is settled upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of the label may be temporary or descriptive for emerging forms; evaluators should be aware the term can be a placeholder while genre definitions evolve.
